title: Describing people: positive and negative qualities
subtitle: shrewd or cunning, thrifty or stingy
summary: Choose precisely between adjectives that describe character, and feel the difference between a positive word like shrewd and its negative twin cunning.

lesson.heading: Character adjectives
lesson.text: Chinese astrology claims that the year you are born in affects your character, and traditional descriptions of the twelve animal years are a rich source of character adjectives. Someone **opportunistic** uses situations for their own benefit; someone **methodical** is systematic and careful; someone **conscientious** takes care to do their work properly.

examples.text: He's rather **opportunistic**. He always tries to use situations to his own advantage.
Rob is a very conscientious and **methodical** worker.
A **chauvinistic** person is too patriotic - Tom thinks his country is better than any other and doesn't listen to reason.

lesson.heading: Adjectives and what they mean
rows: become too excited and lose control
not confident, uncertain about your own abilities
not satisfied if things are not 100% perfect
inclined to say things that upset or offend people
calm, does not easily become excited or angry

lesson.heading: More adjectives and what they mean
rows: a personality that attracts people to you
spends too much money or uses too much of something
thinking of others rather than yourself
inclined to speak in a severe and critical way
without enough experience of life, trusting too easily

lesson.heading: Words that are close but not the same
lesson.text: Many character words come in pairs: one that sounds like praise and one that sounds like criticism. Calling someone **shrewd** compliments their judgement; calling the same person **cunning** suggests they are not honest. Advanced English is full of these choices, so pick the word that carries the attitude you mean.

examples.text: Ellie, my boss, is very **astute** and she can be very **witty**.
I find her assistant David a bit **sullen** and **obstinate**.
Julia is a bit **stingy** and extremely **work-obsessed**.

lesson.heading: Formal and informal synonyms
lesson.text: The longer, Latin-based adjectives belong to formal writing. In friendly conversation people reach for a shorter word instead: **altruistic** becomes unselfish, **parsimonious** becomes thrifty, **industrious** becomes hard-working, **terse** becomes abrupt, and **unscrupulous** becomes dishonest.

examples.text: He was a very **altruistic** person, almost to the point of being **naive**.
She was very **courageous** in speaking out against corruption.
I'm always happy to go out for a meal with Kerstin. She's such **good company**.
examples.note: good company = pleasant and entertaining to spend time with

lesson.text: Shrewd praises judgement; cunning hints at dishonesty. Thrifty praises care with money; stingy condemns it. Same behaviour, different attitude.

exercises.prompt: Sophie is always so calm and never gets excited or angry. Which adjective describes her?
exercises.explanation: Placid means calm, not easily excited or angered.

exercises.prompt: Harry is such a practical and sensible person. Which adjective describes him?
Alice can always be relied upon to make the right decision. Which adjective describes her?
Andrey has a tendency to say things that upset people. Which adjective describes him?
exercises.explanation: A tactless person is inclined to say things that upset or offend people.

exercises.prompt: I wish Tatyana would calm down and not get so ___ away about things.
exercises.explanation: To get carried away is to become too excited and lose control.

exercises.prompt: She has an ___ approach to life rather than a rational one.
exercises.explanation: An intuitive person understands things instinctively.

exercises.prompt: My father was a somewhat quick-tempered and ___ sort of person.
exercises.explanation: Morose means gloomy; sullen is a close synonym.

exercises.prompt: He was a very altruistic person, almost to the point of being ___.
exercises.explanation: Naive means without enough experience of life, trusting too easily.

exercises.prompt: Aisha has a ___ personality. Everyone is drawn to her.
exercises.explanation: A magnetic personality attracts people to you.

exercises.prompt: I find Eva a bit ___ and rude - she speaks in a quick, short way.
exercises.explanation: Brusque means speaking in a quick and rude way; terse is close to it.

exercises.prompt: She's fun-loving but she can be a bit ___ at times - she doesn't care about serious things.
exercises.explanation: A superficial person does not care about serious things.

exercises.prompt: I think Max is ___. He doesn't have much confidence and isn't really sure of himself.
exercises.explanation: Insecure means not confident, uncertain about your own abilities.

exercises.prompt: I'm always happy to go out for a meal with Kerstin. She's such ___.
exercises.hint: (two words: pleasant and entertaining to be with)
exercises.explanation: Someone who is good company is pleasant and entertaining to spend time with.

exercises.prompt: Owen's a ___. He's never happy if he doesn't get an A-grade in every test.
exercises.explanation: A perfectionist is not satisfied if things are not 100% perfect.

exercises.prompt: Match each abstract noun with its adjective.
Match each formal adjective with a more informal synonym.
Does each adjective have positive or negative associations?

exercises.statement: Calling someone dogged is more complimentary than calling them obstinate.
exercises.explanation: Correct - resolute and dogged are positive; stubborn and obstinate are the negative equivalents.

exercises.statement: An extravagant person is careful with money.
exercises.explanation: Extravagant means spending too much money. The careful person is thrifty or frugal.

exercises.prompt: Put this description of a colleague in order.
exercises.answer: Marco is very obliging, supportive and tolerant
exercises.explanation: All three adjectives are positive: ready to help, encouraging, and open-minded.
